section.title: The Genealogy of Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Matthew opens his Gospel where Israel's hope has always pointed: a family tree that runs from Abraham through David to Jesus the Christ. It is not a dry list but a carefully shaped argument, arranged in three sets of fourteen, that Jesus is the promised King and the true seed of Abraham, the one in whom the whole story of Israel finds its goal.
section.thesis: By tracing Jesus back to David and to Abraham, and by folding into the line surprising sinners and outsiders, Matthew announces from his first sentence that Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah, the royal Son who fulfills God's promises and welcomes the unlikely into His story.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the opening title, son of David and son of Abraham; the line from Abraham to David; the royal line from David to the exile; the line from the exile to the Christ; and the summary of three fourteens.

units.label: Son of David, son of Abraham
units.note: the title over the whole Gospel

verses.text: This is the record of the {{geneseos|genealogy}} of Jesus {{christos|Christ}}, the son of {{david|David}}, the son of Abraham:

units.label: From Abraham to David
units.note: the promise carried through the patriarchs

verses.text: Abraham was the {{egennesen|father}} of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers.
Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram.
Ram was the father of Amminadab, Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon.
Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse,
and Jesse the father of David the king. Next: David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife,

units.label: From David to the exile
units.note: the kings of Judah, glory and decline

verses.text: Solomon the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asa.
Asa was the father of Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah.
Uzziah was the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah.
Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh, Manasseh the father of Amon, Amon the father of Josiah,
and Josiah the father of Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon.

units.label: From the exile to the Christ

verses.text: After the exile to Babylon: Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel, Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor.
Azor was the father of Zadok, Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud.
Eliud was the father of Eleazar, Eleazar the father of Matthan, Matthan the father of Jacob,
and Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

units.label: Fourteen, fourteen, fourteen
units.note: the pattern that frames the whole

verses.text: In all, then, there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ.

geneseos.gloss: Origin, birth, genealogy. The opening phrase, biblos geneseos, book of the genealogy, deliberately echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, so that Matthew presents the coming of Jesus as a new beginning, the genesis of the renewed people of God.

christos.gloss: Anointed One, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah. Kings, priests, and prophets were anointed; the title gathers up the hope of the promised King from David's line. Matthew's whole Gospel argues that Jesus is this long-awaited Christ.

david.gloss: David, Israel's greatest king, to whom God promised a son whose throne would last forever, 2 Samuel 7. Son of David becomes a central messianic title in Matthew; the crowds, the blind, and the children will hail Jesus by it.

egennesen.gloss: Begot, was the father of. The verb drums through the list like a heartbeat, generation after generation, until the pattern breaks at verse 16: not Joseph begot Jesus, but of Mary was born Jesus, signaling that this birth is unlike all the others.

basic.context: Matthew begins his Gospel with a family tree. To modern readers a genealogy feels like a place to skip, but to a Jewish reader it was the headline. It answers the first question anyone would ask about a would-be Messiah: who are you, and what is your line? Matthew's answer is that Jesus is the son of David, the rightful King, and the son of Abraham, in whom the nations would be blessed.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical line, but Matthew has shaped it as an argument. He arranges it in three sets of fourteen and even skips some names to make the pattern, which was an accepted way of teaching. The point is not a complete record but a claim: Jesus stands at the climax of Israel's whole story, its promises, its kings, its exile, and its hope of return.
basic.originalLanguages: The first words, book of the genealogy, echo the book of Genesis, hinting at a new beginning. The title Christ means Anointed One, the promised King. The verb father, or begot, repeats down the whole list until it breaks at verse 16, where Jesus is not begotten by Joseph but born of Mary, quietly preparing us for the virgin birth.
basic.typology: Abraham, David, and the exile are not just names but chapters of the one story. Jesus is the seed of Abraham through whom blessing comes to all peoples, the son of David who takes the everlasting throne, and the one who ends the true exile of God's people, their exile from God because of sin.
basic.christ: The whole list exists to name one person: Jesus, who is called Christ. He is the goal of Abraham's line and David's throne. Even the surprising names, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah's wife, show a Messiah who comes for sinners and outsiders, and who is not ashamed to have them in His family.
basic.god: God keeps His promises across a thousand years, through faithful kings and wicked ones, through glory and through the disaster of exile. He is patient, sovereign, and faithful, weaving even human failure and foreign women into the line that leads to the Savior.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12 and 22 promise blessing to the nations through Abraham's seed. 2 Samuel 7 promises David a son whose kingdom lasts forever. Galatians 3 says Christ is the seed of Abraham, and Ruth 4 gives the line from Perez to David that Matthew carries on.
basic.oneStory: Matthew opens the New Testament by tying it firmly to the Old. Every promise to Abraham and David, every hope carried through the kings and the exile, converges on Jesus the Christ. The long wait is over; the King has come, and the door is open to sinners and to the nations.

context.literary:
The first verse is a title, and a loaded one. The Greek phrase biblos geneseos, 'book of origin' or 'book of the generations,' is the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, 'This is the book of the generations of Adam.' Matthew has begun a new Genesis. The verse also reverses the natural order, naming David before Abraham, 'son of David, son of Abraham,' so that the royal claim is stated first and the patriarchal promise follows.

The list is built as a staircase in three flights. The first flight climbs from Abraham to David, the king. The second descends from David to the deportation to Babylon, the fall of the kingdom. The third rises, if quietly, from Babylon to the Christ. Verse 17 states the design in words, and the structure is also a narrative: promise, monarchy and decline, exile and waiting, and the arrival of the one for whom all of it was preparing.

Within the list, Matthew breaks the pattern of 'X the father of Y' at five points. Four women appear, Tamar in verse 3, Rahab and Ruth in verse 5, and 'Uriah's wife' in verse 6. The fifth break is verse 16, where the formula that has run through the whole list changes. Joseph is 'the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus.' The relative pronoun 'whom' is feminine in Greek, so the birth is traced to Mary alone, and the verb is a passive, 'was born,' not the active 'fathered' used before. The chain of begetting is deliberately interrupted at its last link.

The list also pauses on the exile, 'the exile to Babylon,' in verses 11, 12 and 17, so that the reader feels the great rupture. The genealogy ends not with a name that ends the line but with a title, 'Jesus, who is called Christ,' and the reader is invited to see that what was lost at the exile is being recovered. Matthew's Gospel will end with the word 'age,' 'to the very end of the age,' and its first sentence opens the arc.
context.historical:
Genealogies were serious documents in the Judaism of Matthew's day. Returning exiles had been required to prove descent, and some priests who could not were excluded from priestly service, Ezra 2:62. Ancient genealogies, in Israel and in the surrounding world, often skipped generations and gave the names that served the purpose in hand, and the Old Testament does this itself. Matthew's 'father of' means 'ancestor of,' as the opening 'son of David, son of Abraham' shows, since Jesus is plainly not David's immediate son.

Matthew has left out some kings that the Old Testament lists. Between Joram and Uzziah in verse 8 the books of Chronicles name Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah, 1 Chronicles 3:11-12, and between Josiah and Jeconiah in verse 11 stands Jehoiakim, 1 Chronicles 3:15-16. The omissions let Matthew fit his three groups of fourteen, and nobody in his first audience would have called it deception.

The women would have startled first readers, for women were rarely named in Jewish genealogies. The four named are all remembered for irregular circumstances. Tamar conceived by Judah, who acknowledged, 'She is more righteous than I,' Genesis 38:26. Rahab was a Canaanite woman of Jericho who sheltered the spies and was spared, Joshua 6:25. Ruth was a Moabite, one of the Moabite wives of Elimelech's sons, Ruth 1:4. Bathsheba is not named but is described as 'Uriah's wife,' a phrase that draws attention to David's sin, 2 Samuel 11:3. Rahab and Ruth were foreigners by birth, Bathsheba was married to a Hittite, and all four are linked to scandal or to need.

The late first century also brought a pressing question for Matthew's readers. If Jesus was the Christ, where was His claim written down? The title 'son of David' was the title crowds shouted at Jesus, Matthew 21:9, and a Canaanite woman used it in her plea, Matthew 15:22. Matthew's opening response is a document: a line from Abraham that passes through the kings to Joseph, in whose house Jesus is legally born.
context.canonical:
The first verse gathers two promises and holds them together. To Abraham God said that all peoples on earth would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 12:3. To David He swore that one of his descendants would sit on his throne, Psalm 132:11, 2 Samuel 7:12-16. Between these stand Jacob's blessing on Judah, 'The scepter will not depart from Judah ... until Shiloh comes,' Genesis 49:10, and the prophets' picture of a Branch from Jesse's stump, Isaiah 11:1, and a righteous Branch for David, Jeremiah 23:5. Matthew places Jesus at the point where all of these lines meet.

The names in the list come from the Old Testament, so the genealogy is also a reading guide to it. The line from Perez to David is the one given in Ruth 4:18-22 and in 1 Chronicles 2. The kings of verses 6 to 11 are the kings of Judah, whose stories fill Samuel, Kings and Chronicles. The names after Jeconiah are hardly known, since the Old Testament records only Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, who led the return and was promised that God would make him like a signet ring, Haggai 2:23. After Jeconiah, Matthew's last fourteen names include no kings, only the quiet generations of a throne waiting for its heir.

Jeconiah deserves a comment. The prophet Jeremiah said that none of his descendants would sit on David's throne, Jeremiah 22:30. If Jesus were Joseph's biological son, that word would block the claim. Because Matthew insists that Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph, the curse is not violated, though Jesus still inherits the throne's legal right through His adoptive father. Many readers see the genealogy and the birth narrative as each protecting the other.

The New Testament repeatedly cites the line. Paul says Jesus 'was a descendant of David according to the flesh' and was declared Son of God by the resurrection, Romans 1:3-4. Revelation closes with Jesus saying 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16. Luke gives a different genealogy that runs through Nathan, Luke 3:31, and ends at Adam, and the two accounts together present Jesus as King of Israel and as Son of the first man.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote for readers who knew the Scriptures and wanted to know whether Jesus really was the one they promised. He does not argue in the first line; he lines up the names and lets the history carry the case. The first thing he wanted his readers to grasp is that this is the climax of an old story and not a new religion. Every name is a landmark they could check against Genesis, Ruth, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles.

He also wanted them to feel the shape of the story, and the three sets of fourteen are how he does it. The first set is the age of promise rising to the king. The second is the age of the kings falling into exile. The third is the age of waiting. To count is to see that the history is not random. A reader who has just finished the list would be asking where the third set ends, and the last verse answers: with the Christ.

He meant his readers, many of them Jewish and some of them Gentile, to be startled by the women. A Messiah whose family includes a woman who forced her father in law to face his own failure, a Canaanite prostitute who became a believer, a foreign widow, and a king's partner in adultery is a Messiah who has not been protected from the world's mess. The first hearers were meant to see that the One who is called Christ shares His genealogy with sinners, and that those whom Israel's leaders thought of as outsiders already belong to His line. The Great Commission at the end of the Gospel is anticipated by the first page.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
A genealogy records and does not command. Nothing in the list tells the reader what to do. It would be a mistake to treat the irregular unions of Tamar and Judah or of David and Bathsheba as examples to copy, or to claim that God approves of the sins that stand behind some of the names. Matthew records them without comment, and the Old Testament condemns the worst of them, as when Nathan confronts David, 2 Samuel 12. What the text shows is that God's purpose is not defeated by human failure, not that human failure is acceptable.

The tidy fourteens are also a descriptive structure and not a model. Readers are not meant to pad their own family histories to fit a pattern, and the omission of several kings is not a precedent for sloppiness. It shows that the genealogy served a theological and memorable purpose and that its first readers understood that.

What carries forward is the conviction that Jesus is the Messiah and King, and a posture that follows from it. If the One whose line includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba is the Savior, then no history is too tangled for grace, and no one needs to hide behind respectability. The text invites worship, humility and a welcome to those who feel that they are outside.

debates.question: Why are Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah's wife included in a royal genealogy?

views.label: They highlight grace to sinners and outsiders
views.case: Several were Gentiles or were touched by scandal; their presence signals that Jesus' kingdom will reach the morally broken and the non-Jew, anticipating the great commission to all nations.

views.label: They show God's providence through irregular unions
views.case: Each woman advanced the line in an unexpected, even improper way, underscoring that God, not human respectability, preserved the promised seed.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on grace: the Messiah's own family tree is stitched together from outsiders and sinners, so no one need think themselves too far from His kingdom.

debates.question: How do we handle the neat three-times-fourteen pattern when names are clearly omitted?

views.label: A deliberate mnemonic and theological device
views.case: Fourteen is the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew, and structuring the list around it foregrounds Jesus as the son of David; selective omission for symmetry was a normal ancient practice, not an error.

views.label: A strict count that must be defended literally
views.case: Some seek to reconcile every generation as a full record, but this strains the text; the count of father to son in the ancient sense allows for representative selection.

debates.bearing: The structure is a teaching aid, not a modern registry; recognizing this guards us from false problems and lets the intended message, Jesus the son of David, ring clear.

debates.question: Why does Luke's genealogy differ from Matthew's?

views.label: Luke gives Mary's line, Matthew gives Joseph's
views.case: Luke 3:23 says Jesus was 'regarded as the son of Joseph, the son of Heli,' and some read the list as Mary's family through her father, with Joseph named as son-in-law. On this view Matthew gives the legal line through Joseph and Luke the physical line through Mary, and Luke's line passes through David's son Nathan, Luke 3:31.

views.label: Both give Joseph's line, joined by a levirate or adoptive link
views.case: Others hold that both lists run through Joseph, with a levirate marriage or adoption explaining the different fathers named at points where the two lists cross, as at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. They note that the text never says Luke's list is Mary's.

views.label: The lists serve different theological purposes
views.case: A third approach asks less about reconciling every name and more about what each evangelist is doing: Matthew presents the royal Messiah of Israel, and Luke the Savior of all humanity, tracing to Adam.

debates.bearing: No proposal can be proved from the text alone, and the early church did not treat the difference as an embarrassment. What the two lists share is the claim that matters: Jesus belongs to David's house and to the whole human family.

study.originalLanguages:
The Greek of the passage is simple, which is why its few changes of pattern stand out. Start with the title in verse 1, biblos geneseos. The second word is the one that gives Genesis its Greek name, and it is also used for the 'generations' formulas that structure that book, Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. Matthew may be heard as saying, 'This is the book of the new beginning of Jesus Christ.' Whether he meant the title for the genealogy alone or for the whole Gospel is debated, and the answer may be both.

The second is Christos. It is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, 'anointed one.' In the Old Testament, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil, and the title was gradually narrowed to the coming king from David's line. Matthew uses it as a name in verse 1, 'Jesus Christ,' as a title in verse 16, 'who is called Christ,' and as a definite title in verse 17, 'the Christ,' so the reader moves from a name to a claim.

The third is the verb of the list, egennesen. It is an active aorist, 'fathered,' and it is repeated at each link. Its last form is the surprise. In verse 16 Matthew writes, 'Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus.' The verb changes to a passive, egennethe, 'was born,' and the relative pronoun is feminine singular. The grammar itself says that Jesus came from Mary and that Joseph was the husband and not the father. Joseph is called the 'husband,' the same word, aner, used again in Matthew 1:19.

The fourth is the word for the exile. In verses 11, 12 and 17 the BSB's 'exile to Babylon' is a Greek noun that means a forced removal or deportation, and it is used three times to mark the great turning. The exile is the hinge of the whole structure.

The fifth is the remarkable naming of the women. Matthew writes Thamar, Rhachab and Routh with no description, and for the fourth he writes 'the one of Uriah,' a form that leaves the name Bathsheba unsaid and says only whose wife she had been. The omission is pointed: the reader supplies the name and the sin. Notice also that in verse 3 and verse 5 the phrase is 'by Tamar' and 'by Rahab,' using the preposition ek, 'out of,' which signals that these women are the source from which the line proceeded.

The sixth is the word 'son,' huios. 'Son of David, son of Abraham' means a descendant and heir, not an immediate child. The title Son of David is Matthew's favourite way of naming Jesus' royal identity, and it recurs in the cries of the blind men, Matthew 9:27 and 20:30, in the Canaanite woman's plea, and in the crowd's shout, Matthew 21:9.

typology.fulfillment: God promised Abraham that 'all peoples on earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, and later through his offspring, Genesis 22:18. Matthew names Abraham in the first line and lists Isaac and Jacob and Judah in the next, as though each were a rung on the ladder of the promise. Paul states what Matthew implies: the promise was spoken to Abraham and 'to his seed,' meaning One, who is Christ, Galatians 3:16, and those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, Galatians 3:29. The escalation is that the one seed becomes a family drawn from all nations. The type falls short because Isaac could be a bearer of the promise but not its fulfilment.

typology.type: The royal line and the Son of David
typology.fulfillment: David and his sons are the type of the king who will rule rightly. Solomon is called by the text a son of David and builds the temple, and Jesus says 'One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42. The promise that David's throne would be established for ever, 2 Samuel 7:13, is fulfilled in the one who reigns and whose kingdom has no end, Luke 1:32-33. The escalation is that the earthly kings declined, reaching the point of exile, and the final king never fails. The type falls short at the fall: every king in the list, even the best, died and left a throne that could be taken.

The deportation to Babylon is the hinge of the list, and Israel's return under Zerubbabel was only a partial recovery. Matthew's third fourteen leads not to a restored kingdom but to a person. In Jesus the true return begins: He is the one who will 'save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, and the exile from God is the deeper bondage. The type is incomplete because the return under Persian rule left Israel still under foreign power, while the Christ delivers from sin and death.

typology.type: The women as signs of the nations and of grace
typology.fulfillment: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba are not types in the strict sense, but they function as signs. Rahab was spared when Jericho fell, Joshua 6:25, and Ruth entered Israel and found a redeemer, Ruth 4:14. Their inclusion points forward to the Gentiles who come to the King, the magi of the next chapter and the Canaanite woman who cried 'Son of David.' The escalation in Christ is that foreigners do not join the line by exception; the nations are invited into the family through Him, Matthew 28:19. The correspondence is limited by the fact that these women were exceptions in Israel's history, and in Christ the exception becomes the rule.

study.christ:
The genealogy leads to Christ in the most direct way a text can: it names Him as its destination. Everything before verse 16 is a road, and the road ends at 'Jesus, who is called Christ.' The question of the first page is who this is, and the answer is that He is the one for whom the list was written.

It leads to Him by promise. God's word to Abraham was that blessing would come to the nations through his offspring, and His oath to David was that one of his descendants would reign for ever. Matthew sets both in the title of verse 1 and then shows by the list that the road runs through real history, not a myth. Paul says that Jesus is the seed to whom the promise was made, Galatians 3:16, and that in Him the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles, Galatians 3:14.

It leads to Him by the structure of the three fourteens. The sum of the three sets is forty-two, and after Jeconiah the third set holds no king at all. The new David is the one who comes at the end of the waiting, when the house of David has been reduced to a family of builders and craftsmen. The King does not arrive from a palace but from a carpenter's household, which prepares the reader for the manger and the cross.

It leads to Him by the women. The Christ who is called the Son of David has among His ancestors a deceiver who was found to be in the right, a prostitute who was saved by faith, a foreign widow who found a kinsman redeemer, and the woman whose husband David had killed. He is not ashamed of them. The writer to the Hebrews says, 'Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. This is the same Jesus who sits at table with tax collectors and sinners, Matthew 9:10-13. A genealogy of sinners is the right prelude to a Savior of sinners.

And it leads to Him by the grammar of verse 16. The chain of fathers breaks at the last link, and Matthew's relative pronoun points to Mary alone. That is how the line of David can be passed on to a child whom David's heir did not father. Joseph names Him, Matthew 1:25, and so adopts Him into David's house, but the birth is from God. Paul says, 'God sent His Son, born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4.

A word of care is needed. Not every name in the list is a hidden picture of Jesus, and the details of each king's life do not have to be read as a code. The link rests on the promises the New Testament itself says are fulfilled in Jesus, and on Matthew's own insistence that the Messiah is the point.
study.god:
The first thing the genealogy says about God is that He keeps promises across time. A thousand years lie between Abraham and the Christ in this list. The same God who promised blessing to the nations is the God who is seen carrying that promise through a family with famine, slavery, judges, kings and exile. He does not forget in the long stretches when nothing seems to happen.

It shows a God who is sovereign over human history without being its author in the sense of approving all that is done. The tangled stories behind the names, Judah's failure with Tamar, David's sin with Bathsheba, the wicked kings, are real sins, and Matthew does not excuse them. Yet God steers through them, so that nothing human wickedness does can cancel His purpose. Joseph the patriarch said it plainly: 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good,' Genesis 50:20. The genealogy shows this at the scale of a whole line.

It shows a God who is generous to outsiders. The women who enter the line are not there because Israel deserved them. They came from Canaan, Moab and the house of a Hittite, and God took them in. The tenderness is not an afterthought, because the book of Ruth, which Matthew's readers knew, ends with a Moabite great grandmother of David. The God of this genealogy is not the property of one nation, and He has been welcoming the unlikely from the start.

It shows God as patient with judgment. The exile is not hidden. The list admits that the kingdom fell, and the Old Testament says why, in the failures of kings and people. Yet the exile is not the last word: after the exile, the line continues and arrives. The God who judges is the God who preserves, so that Jeremiah can say both 'Enroll this man as childless' and, in the next chapter, 'I will raise up for David a righteous Branch,' Jeremiah 22:30 and 23:5.

For worship, this means praise for a God who keeps His word and whose faithfulness does not depend on ours. It also means humility, because the line that arrives at the Savior includes people no one would have chosen. We do not worship a God whose plans collapse when His people fail, and we do not need to pretend that our own history is tidier than it is.

crossReferences.note: The Greek Old Testament uses the same words at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, 'the book of the generations,' that Matthew uses in his first verse. The echo marks his book as the opening of a new creation story, with Jesus Christ as its beginning.

Judah admits that Tamar is more righteous than he is. The shameful story that lies behind the name in Matthew 1:3 shows that the line of the Messiah passes through a moment in which the patriarch had to confess his failing.

Joshua spares Rahab and her household because she hid the spies, and she lives among the Israelites. Matthew's list mentions her by name, and the New Testament praises her faith, so a Canaanite woman stands in the Messiah's ancestry.

The Moabite Ruth marries Boaz and bears Obed, who is the father of Jesse, the father of David. The women of Bethlehem bless the LORD for a kinsman redeemer, and the little family story becomes a royal one.

David inquires about the woman, and is told she is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Matthew's phrase 'Uriah's wife' recalls the whole story of adultery and murder, and it shows that the Messianic line is not kept clean by the king's own conduct.

The Chronicler's list of David's descendants through Solomon to Jeconiah is the source for Matthew's second fourteen, and it names the kings that Matthew left out, which shows that the omission was a choice.

Jeremiah says none of Jeconiah's descendants will prosper on David's throne. Because Matthew's list passes through Jeconiah, and Jesus is born of Mary and not fathered by Joseph, the verse sets up the question that the next section answers.
God says He will make Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel like His signet ring. Zerubbabel is in Matthew's third set, and the promise to him is a sign that the line of David was not rejected for ever.

Luke's genealogy runs backward from Jesus through Nathan, a son of David, all the way to Adam and God. Read together with Matthew's, it shows Jesus as King of Israel and as the Son who belongs to all humanity.

Paul says that Jesus was a descendant of David according to the flesh and was declared the Son of God with power by the resurrection. It is the same pair of claims, royal descent and divine sonship, that Matthew sets side by side in chapters 1 and 2.

The crowds shout 'Hosanna to the Son of David' as Jesus enters Jerusalem. It shows that the title in Matthew 1:1 was heard by the people as a claim to kingship, and it turns the first line of the Gospel into a public cry.

Jesus calls Himself 'the Root and the Offspring of David.' The Bible's last chapter repeats the claim of its first New Testament page, and the royal line is both the ancestor and the descendant of David.

study.oneStory:
The genealogy is a compact retelling of the story so far, and it picks up threads that were left hanging at the end of the Old Testament. In the garden God said that a seed of the woman would crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15. To Abraham He promised a seed through whom all nations would be blessed. To Judah He gave the scepter, and to David a house that would stand for ever. The prophets then spoke of a Branch. Matthew gathers all these promises and says, in the form of a list, that they have a single answer.

It answers the question left by the exile. The kingdom fell, the temple was burned, and the descendants of David were no longer on the throne. The prophets had said that the house would rise again, and the long postexilic silence seemed to deny it. By naming the third set of fourteen and ending at Jesus, Matthew says that the silence was not the end. The hidden years of the carpenter's family are the years of a seed growing.

It sets up the rest of the Gospel. The title Son of David returns throughout, in the cries of the needy and in the Hosannas of the crowd, and the title Son of Abraham looks ahead to the nations: the wise men come from the east, Matthew 2:1, a centurion's faith is praised above Israel's, Matthew 8:10-11, and the Gospel ends with the command to make disciples of all nations. The inclusion of Gentile women is a first sign of that ending.

It also sets up the cross. The line of kings that began with David and fell into exile is the line that produces a king who will be crowned with thorns. The Messiah's family tree contains betrayal, adultery, murder and failure, and the Messiah will take these on Himself. What the genealogy shows in family history, the cross accomplishes in reality: the sin of those in the line is borne by the one at its end.

It ends in the new creation. The seed who is the son of David and the son of Abraham becomes the one who sits on the throne for ever, and the Gospel's final verse promises His presence to the end of the age. In Revelation a great multitude from every nation stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and the Root of David is the Lamb who has conquered, Revelation 5:5-6. The family tree that began with Abraham at the first verse of the New Testament finds its last branch in a redeemed people from every tongue, all of whom are counted as children of the promise.

quiz.q: What two titles does Matthew give Jesus in the opening verse?

options.text: The son of David and the son of Abraham.
options.note: Verse 1 names both, framing Jesus as the royal Messiah and the seed of promise.

options.text: The son of David, the promised King.
options.note: True and central, but it leaves out son of Abraham, the other title Matthew highlights.

options.text: The son of Adam and the Savior of the world.
options.note: That is closer to Luke's emphasis; Matthew's opening titles are son of David and son of Abraham.

options.text: The son of Moses and the giver of the law.
options.note: Matthew never calls Jesus son of Moses; the opening titles are son of David and son of Abraham.

quiz.q: Why does Matthew include Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah's wife in the line?

options.text: To show a Messiah whose family includes sinners and outsiders, a sign of grace.
options.note: Their presence anticipates a kingdom that reaches the broken and the nations.

options.text: To record God's providence through unexpected, irregular events.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it understates the deliberate theme of grace to outsiders.

options.text: Simply to be historically complete about the mothers.
options.note: Genealogies normally omitted women; naming these four is pointed, not mere completeness.

options.text: To prove the line was ritually pure and unblemished.
options.note: The opposite: these names carry scandal and foreignness, highlighting grace, not purity.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the three sets of fourteen generations?

options.text: A deliberate structure foregrounding Jesus as the son of David, the number of David's name.
options.note: Verse 17 states the pattern; fourteen ties the whole list to David and to Messiah.

options.text: A memory aid that organizes Israel's long history into stages.
options.note: True, it aids memory, but it misses the pointed link to David and the Messiah.

options.text: A precise count of every single ancestor without omission.
options.note: Matthew clearly omits some names to make the pattern; it is representative, not exhaustive.

options.text: An accidental coincidence with no intended meaning.
options.note: Verse 17 makes the pattern explicit and intentional, not accidental.

quiz.q: How does the wording change at verse 16, and why does it matter?

options.text: The chain of begot breaks: Joseph is husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, hinting at the virgin birth.
options.note: The grammar refuses to say Joseph begot Jesus, preparing for the conception by the Spirit.

options.text: Joseph is called the father of Jesus, completing the royal line.
options.note: Joseph gives Jesus legal Davidic descent, but the text pointedly avoids saying he begot Jesus.

options.text: Mary is named as a descendant of David directly.
options.note: Matthew traces the line through Joseph, not through Mary's descent, in this passage.

options.text: The verse says Jesus begot the next generation.
options.note: The list ends with Jesus; He is the goal, not a link to further generations here.

quiz.q: What does the genealogy reveal about God?

options.text: He faithfully keeps His promises across centuries, through both faithful and sinful people.
options.note: The line preserves the promises to Abraham and David through every generation.

options.text: He works only through the strong and successful kings.
options.note: God did work through kings, but the list is full of failures and outsiders too, so this is too narrow.

options.text: He rewards only the morally pure ancestors.
options.note: The line includes notorious sinners; the theme is grace and faithfulness, not moral reward.

options.text: He had abandoned His promises during the exile.
options.note: The exile is a low point, yet God preserves the line through it, showing He never abandoned His word.

questions: Matthew's first word about Jesus is His lineage, His belonging to a story bigger than Himself. How does it steady your faith to know Jesus stands at the climax of a thousand years of God keeping His promises?
The family tree of the Messiah is full of sinners and outsiders. What does it mean for you that Jesus was not ashamed to have such people in His line, and to seek such people still?
God preserved the promised line even through the disaster of exile. Where in your own life do you need to trust that God is keeping His purposes alive even in seasons that feel like loss?
The whole list exists to point to one name, Jesus the Christ. In what ways are you tempted to make the story about yourself rather than about Him?
Jesus is the son of Abraham, in whom the nations are blessed. How does this shape the way you pray for and reach people who are far from God?

translationNotes.note: The record of the genealogy renders biblos geneseos, literally book of the genealogy or of the origin, a phrase that echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1.
Uriah's wife names Bathsheba without naming her, keeping the memory of David's sin in view even as the royal line continues through Solomon.
Jeconiah is also called Jehoiachin; the list telescopes some generations, a normal ancient practice, to preserve the pattern of three sets of fourteen.
